questions.q: A matrix has 24 elements. How many different orders can it have?
questions.solution:
An order $m \times n$ needs $mn = 24$, so count the ordered factor pairs of 24:

$(1,24), (2,12), (3,8), (4,6), (6,4), (8,3), (12,2), (24,1)$ — **8** of them.

Think of 24 chairs to be set out in a perfect rectangle: every different rectangle you can make, counting a $3\times8$ hall as different from an $8\times3$ one, is one order.

questions.q: If $A$ is any square matrix, then $A + A^{T}$ is always:
questions.solution:
Let $B = A + A^{T}$. Then $B^{T} = A^{T} + (A^{T})^{T} = A^{T} + A = B$, which is the definition of **symmetric**.

Adding a matrix to its own mirror image across the diagonal balances the two halves — fold the page along the diagonal and the numbers land on their equals.

questions.q: If $A$ is of order $3 \times 4$ and $B$ is of order $4 \times 2$, then the order of $AB$ is:
questions.solution:
Multiplication is allowed when the inner numbers match: $3 \times \underline{4}$ and $\underline{4} \times 2$. They do.

The product keeps the **outer** numbers: $\mathbf{3 \times 2}$.

Like joining two pipes: the ends that meet must be the same width, and the pipe you end up with has the outer two openings.

questions.q: Every diagonal element of a skew-symmetric matrix is:
questions.solution:
Skew-symmetric means $a_{ij} = -a_{ji}$. Put $i = j$: $a_{ii} = -a_{ii}$, so $2a_{ii} = 0$ and $a_{ii} = \mathbf{0}$.

A diagonal entry is its own mirror image, and the only number that is the negative of itself is zero.

questions.q: If a matrix $A$ is both symmetric and skew-symmetric, then $A$ is:
questions.solution:
Symmetric gives $A^{T} = A$; skew-symmetric gives $A^{T} = -A$.

So $A = -A \Rightarrow 2A = O \Rightarrow A = \mathbf{O}$, the zero matrix.

Only one thing equals its own opposite, and it is nothing at all.

questions.q: If $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$, find the element in the second row, second column of $AB$.
questions.solution:
The $(2,2)$ entry pairs **row 2 of $A$** with **column 2 of $B$**:

$(3)(0) + (4)(3) = 0 + 12 = \mathbf{12}$.

Row across, column down, multiply the partners, add — you never need the rest of the product to answer for one cell.

questions.q: If $\begin{pmatrix} x + y & 7 \\ 5 & x - y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 7 \\ 5 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, find the value of $x$.
questions.solution:
Equal matrices match entry by entry, like two identical seating plans.

$x + y = 8$ and $x - y = 2$. Adding: $2x = 10$, so $x = \mathbf{5}$ (and $y = 3$).

$A^{2} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

That is $2A$, so $k = \mathbf{2}$.

In general, for this matrix $A^{n} = 2^{\,n-1}A$ — each multiplication doubles it, never changes its shape.

questions.q: How many different $3 \times 3$ matrices can be formed whose every entry is either $0$ or $1$?
questions.solution:
There are $3 \times 3 = 9$ cells, and each is an independent two-way switch.

$2^{9} = \mathbf{512}$.

Nine light switches on a wall: every on/off pattern is one matrix.

questions.q: If $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$, find the sum of all the elements of $A + A^{T}$.
questions.solution:
$A^{T} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ -1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$, so $A + A^{T} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 8 \end{pmatrix}$.

Sum of the entries $= 4 + 2 + 2 + 8 = \mathbf{16}$.

Quicker route: transposing moves entries around but never changes their total, so the entries of $A + A^{T}$ add to twice the total of $A$ — and $2 - 1 + 3 + 4 = 8$, giving $16$.

questions.q: Express $A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix.
questions.solution:
Every square matrix splits as $A = \tfrac12\left(A + A^{T}\right) + \tfrac12\left(A - A^{T}\right)$ — the balanced part plus the unbalanced part.

$A^{T} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 5 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$.

**Symmetric part:** $\tfrac12\left(A + A^{T}\right) = \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 6 & 6 \\ 6 & -2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 3 \\ 3 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$.

**Skew-symmetric part:** $\tfrac12\left(A - A^{T}\right) = \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.

**Check:** the two add back to $A$. ✓

It is the same trick as writing a number as its average with a partner plus the half-difference — one piece symmetric, one piece signed.

$A^{2} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 5 \\ -5 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$.

(First entry: $3(3) + 1(-1) = 8$; then $3(1) + 1(2) = 5$; $-1(3) + 2(-1) = -5$; $-1(1) + 2(2) = 3$.)

$5A = \begin{pmatrix} 15 & 5 \\ -5 & 10 \end{pmatrix}$ and $7I = \begin{pmatrix} 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 \end{pmatrix}$.

$A^{2} - 5A + 7I = \begin{pmatrix} 8 - 15 + 7 & 5 - 5 + 0 \\ -5 + 5 + 0 & 3 - 10 + 7 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = O$. ✓

This is the Cayley–Hamilton identity for this matrix: every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation.

questions.q: Find the matrix $X$ such that $2A + 3X = 5B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix} -3 & 5 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$.
questions.solution:
Rearrange exactly as you would a number equation:

$3X = 5B - 2A \Rightarrow X = \tfrac13\left(5B - 2A\right)$.

$5B = \begin{pmatrix} 20 & 5 \\ 10 & 15 \end{pmatrix}$, $\quad 2A = \begin{pmatrix} -6 & 10 \\ 4 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

$5B - 2A = \begin{pmatrix} 26 & -5 \\ 6 & 13 \end{pmatrix}$.

$X = \tfrac13\begin{pmatrix} 26 & -5 \\ 6 & 13 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac{26}{3} & -\tfrac{5}{3} \\ 2 & \tfrac{13}{3} \end{pmatrix}$.

Matrices add and scale entry by entry, so the algebra is ordinary algebra done 4 times at once.

$AB = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 4 & 11 \end{pmatrix}$, so $(AB)^{T} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 11 \end{pmatrix}$.

$B^{T} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $A^{T} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$.

$B^{T}A^{T} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 11 \end{pmatrix}$. ✓

The **order reverses**, and that is the whole point: taking off a coat and then a shirt undoes dressing in the opposite order to putting them on.

questions.q: Show that for any square matrix $A$, the matrix $A - A^{T}$ is skew-symmetric.
questions.solution:
Let $B = A - A^{T}$. Take the transpose:

$B^{T} = \left(A - A^{T}\right)^{T} = A^{T} - \left(A^{T}\right)^{T} = A^{T} - A$.

But $A^{T} - A = -\left(A - A^{T}\right) = -B$.

$B^{T} = -B$ is precisely the definition of **skew-symmetric**. ∎

Two facts do all the work: transpose distributes over subtraction, and $\left(A^{T}\right)^{T} = A$ — a mirror image of a mirror image is the original.
